title: Lists & Tuples
summary: Ordered collections — lists you can change, and tuples you can't.

checkpoints.title: Mutable lists, immutable tuples
checkpoints.content: A list, `nums = [1, 2, 3]`, can grow, shrink, or change after creation — `nums.append(4)` adds to it in place. A tuple, `point = (3, 4)`, looks similar but can never be changed once created — there's no `.append()` for tuples.
checkpoints.explanation: Tuples are often used for values that shouldn't change, like coordinates — trying to mutate one raises a TypeError.

hints.H0: Square brackets make a list; parentheses make a tuple.
hints.H1: Only lists support methods like .append() that change the collection in place.
hints.H2: Tuples are fixed once created — that's the whole point of using one.

checkpoints.title: Predict a list after append

options.explanation: .append() adds the new item to the end of the list, in place.

options.text: ["apple", "banana"] — append() returns a new list without changing the original
options.explanation: .append() modifies the original list directly — it doesn't return a separate new one.
.append() always adds to the end of the list, never the front.

checkpoints.explanation: .append() mutates the list in place, adding the argument as the new last element.

hints.H0: .append() changes the original list — it doesn't create a copy.
hints.H1: New items always go on the end, not the beginning.

checkpoints.title: Access the last item
checkpoints.content: Given `nums = [10, 20, 30, 40]`, write an expression that gets the last item without knowing the list's length.
checkpoints.explanation: Negative indexes count from the end — -1 is always the last item, -2 the second-to-last, and so on.

hints.H0: Python lets you index from the end using negative numbers.
hints.H1: The very last item is always at index -1.

checkpoints.title: Predict a tuple mutation attempt

options.text: It raises a TypeError — tuples don't support item assignment.
options.explanation: Tuples are immutable, so any attempt to assign into an index fails at runtime.
That would be true for a list — tuples specifically forbid changing their contents this way.

options.text: Nothing happens — the assignment is silently ignored
options.explanation: Python doesn't silently ignore this — it raises an actual error rather than failing quietly.

checkpoints.explanation: Tuples are immutable by design — Python raises TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment.

hints.H0: Recall what makes a tuple different from a list.
hints.H1: Immutability means Python will actively stop you, not just ignore the change.
